newsitem.title: FRANCE: French conscription heads for the scrap-heap.
newsitem.headline: French conscription heads for the scrap-heap.

text.p: France's military conscription marched a step closer to the scrap-heap on Tuesday with a parliamentary debate on a controversial bill which would replace it with a five-day civic lecture.

"I am asking you to approve a national service project which will be passionately part of the (French) Republic and absolutely modern," Defence Minister Charles Millon said when the three-day debate began.

The plan, which involves abolishing conscription in 2002, is part of a move towards all-professional armed forces designed to modernise the military and increase its capacity for long-term action overseas.
Both opposition Socialists and members of the centre-right UDF, junior partner in the ruling coalition, have criticised Millon's reform of military service.
"It's quite normal that the end of military service should prompt nostalgia," Millon said in an interview on RTL radio.
But he added: "We have to set up defences which correspond to our needs -- we have to move to a professional army."

Opposition and government deputies in the National Assembly, the lower house, have pushed through 300 amendments for debate -- one calling for conscription to be reinstated at any time if necessary. Voting on the bill is set for next Tuesday.

Asked whether the government would accept such changes, Millon said: "Conscription hasn't been abolished in the bill. It still exists. We're creating a new system which will allow...young people to commit themselves voluntarily."

Conscription, dating back to 1793, takes in more than 400,000 men every year. Its duration was gradually cut to under a year as it became increasingly unpopular among young men who felt they were wasting time better spent looking for jobs.

The bill says all young people would be subject to a census at the age of 16 and then, between 18 and 25, would be summoned to a five-day "rendez-vous citoyen" (civic meeting) for a course on Republican institutions and defence.

Several senior army officers have privately criticised the new civic meetings as teaching too little and costing too much -- an estimated 1.8 billion francs ($360 million) a year, or almost the price of a nuclear-powered aircraft-carrier over the six years of the defence procurement budget.

The ruling coalition, with its big parliamentary majority, is expected to push the reform through. The Assembly's defence commission, however, has already changed the bill to stress that defence is to be the main aim of the civic meetings and that conscription was only suspended. The meetings would start this year for men and in 2003 for women.

Under an overhaul ordered by President Jacques Chirac last February, France's overall military strength is to drop from half a million to 350,000 when the move to all-professional forces is completed in 2002. The number of troops serving abroad will be cut from 56,000 to 39,000.
